claude_take: Today's set keeps circling one idea: bigger and older isn't holding up. DeepSeek's smaller Flash model just retired its own flagship, and Moonshot's lean, cut-rate Kimi K3 is out-executing labs many times its size, while at the box office a legacy sequel could only limp past a six-week-old blockbuster with a soft opening. Meanwhile the institutions built on inherited authority -- a founder's son at war with the eyewear empire his father built, federal agents using force against unarmed neighbors -- are the ones actually losing control of their own story. If there's a lesson in all this, it's that legacy is buying a lot less patience these days than lean execution is.
claude_take_title: Legacy Is Buying Less Patience Than Execution

items.headline: Moonshot AI Targets $2 Billion in Annual Revenue as Kimi K3 Undercuts US Rivals
items.summary: Moonshot AI, maker of the open-weight Kimi K3 model, told investors its annualized revenue jumped from $300 million in June to over $1 billion in August, and it is now targeting $2 billion by year-end. The surge is powered by Kimi K3's benchmark-topping performance at a fraction of the price of US frontier models, as Moonshot raises funds toward a $50 billion valuation ahead of a planned Hong Kong IPO. It is a concrete sign that Chinese open-weight labs are starting to erode the pricing power of OpenAI and Anthropic, even though their revenues still dwarf Moonshot's.

items.headline: DeepSeek's V4.1-Flash Beats Its Own Flagship, Prompting an Early Retirement for V4-Pro
items.summary: DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash, a 552-billion-parameter model built on a new encoder-decoder architecture that uses roughly a third as many active parameters as its larger V4-Pro flagship yet outperforms it on coding and agentic benchmarks like Terminal-Bench 2.1. The result is striking enough that DeepSeek is retiring V4-Pro from its API starting September 14, routing all traffic to the smaller, cheaper model instead. It is the latest sign that architecture and efficiency gains, not just raw scale, are driving the next round of open-weight model competition.

items.headline: May el-Toukhy's 'Woman Unknown' Wins the Golden Lion at Venice
items.summary: The Danish drama, set in the aftermath of Nazi occupation, took the top prize at the 83rd Venice Film Festival, with lead Mathilde Arcel also winning Best Actress -- a rare double win, and only the eighth time a woman has solely directed the Golden Lion winner. John Malkovich took Best Actor for the CIA comedy 'Wild Horse Nine,' and Ilya Khrzhanovsky's 'DAU' won the Silver Lion for direction. The results give an early shape to the fall awards conversation as the festival circuit moves on to Toronto.

items.headline: 'Practical Magic 2' Ends Spider-Man's Six-Week Reign With a Soft $28-30 Million Opening
items.summary: Warner Bros./Alcon's legacy sequel took the No. 1 spot in its first weekend, finally dethroning 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' after six straight weeks atop the box office. The opening, while more than double what the 1998 original made, still landed below tracking expectations for the $75-million-budgeted film, as the broader post-summer box office gets off to a sluggish start. It is an early read on how much drawing power legacy-brand sequels retain once the summer tentpoles clear out.

items.headline: Pew Finds Roughly 8 in 10 Americans Now Take a Dietary Supplement
items.summary: A new Pew Research Center survey of 3,554 US adults finds about 80% currently take at least one supplement, with usage climbing from 67% of adults under 30 to 85% of those 65 and older. Vitamins and minerals remain the most common, taken by two-thirds of adults, followed by protein powders, omega oils, and herbal supplements. The finding puts hard numbers on how deeply supplement-taking, and the roughly $210 billion industry behind it, has become an ordinary part of American health habits.

items.headline: ICE Agents Clash Violently With Protesters After 40-Hour Frederick, Maryland Standoff
items.summary: Federal immigration agents staked out a residential Frederick neighborhood for about 40 hours after a man fled a traffic stop; when residents linked arms Friday night to block agents from a house, agents charged the crowd, used vehicles to clear sidewalks, and struck at least one protester with a baton. No arrests were made, but the confrontation, caught on video, has drawn demands for investigation from Maryland's congressional delegation and civil-rights groups, amplifying the national fight over ICE conduct during the current enforcement surge.

items.headline: EssilorLuxottica Executives Publicly Rally Behind CEO as Founder's Son Escalates Feud
items.summary: Twenty senior EssilorLuxottica executives signed an unusual memo defending CEO Francesco Milleri after Leonardo Maria Del Vecchio, son of Luxottica's late founder, resigned as Ray-Ban chairman and chief strategy officer and publicly criticized Milleri's pay and management style. The rift, simmering since a June dispute over the family holding company Delfin, is a rare public governance crisis at the world's largest eyewear group, whose brands include Ray-Ban and Oakley alongside license deals with Chanel, Prada, and Armani. It raises real questions about succession and founder-family control just as the stock has fallen more than 50% since November.

items.headline: Heidegger's Enframing (Gestell)
items.summary: In 'The Question Concerning Technology,' Martin Heidegger argued that the danger of modern technology is not the machines themselves but 'Enframing' (Gestell) -- a way of seeing the entire world, including people, as raw material to be ordered, measured, and put to use. Under Enframing, a river becomes a hydroelectric resource and a person becomes 'human resources' before anything else. Heidegger thought escaping this mindset requires cultivating a more contemplative relationship to things, valuing them beyond their usefulness -- a concern that only sharpens as more of daily life gets optimized and quantified by algorithmic systems.
items.summary_fr: Dans « La question de la technique », Martin Heidegger soutient que le danger de la technique moderne ne vient pas des machines elles-mêmes mais de l'arraisonnement (Gestell), une manière de voir le monde entier, y compris les êtres humains, comme un simple stock de ressources à organiser et exploiter. Sous l'arraisonnement, une rivière devient une réserve hydroélectrique et une personne devient d'abord des « ressources humaines ». Pour Heidegger, échapper à cette logique suppose de cultiver un rapport plus contemplatif aux choses, en les valorisant au-delà de leur seule utilité — une inquiétude qui ne fait que s'aiguiser à mesure que la vie quotidienne se retrouve optimisée et quantifiée par des systèmes algorithmiques.
